cues.spoken_span: The three checks use a later fill and two session halves. They ask the same basic question from three angles: does the result hold when the trade arrives differently?

cues.purpose: A signal-to-fill arrow makes the one-bar-later fill stress concrete.
cues.spoken_span: A fill is the price the trade gets when the order enters or exits. Imagine a signal at the end of a bar: the fill is the price attached to the actual entry or exit.

cues.purpose: A signal-to-fill arrow makes the one-bar-later fill stress concrete.
cues.spoken_span: A backtest often uses the signal price as if that were the fill. That is convenient for calculation, but it can make a trade look cleaner than the path a real order takes.

cues.purpose: A signal-to-fill arrow makes the one-bar-later fill stress concrete.
cues.spoken_span: Slippage is the gap between the price you expect and the price you get. A small gap changes the dollars won or lost on every trade, so a long run can feel that gap many times.

cues.purpose: A signal-to-fill arrow makes the one-bar-later fill stress concrete.
cues.spoken_span: Here the test moves the entry one bar in the same direction. That gives the fill price a simple stress. Every candidate gets the same treatment, which makes the comparison repeatable.

cues.purpose: A signal-to-fill arrow makes the one-bar-later fill stress concrete.
cues.spoken_span: The test answers one question about the fill. The test does not model every broker or every order. The controlled comparison is valuable on its own. It says nothing about a particular execution desk.

cues.purpose: Two axes separate time latency from price slippage without conflating them.
cues.spoken_span: Latency is the time from the signal to the fill. If the market moves while an order is waiting, that time can change the price of the trade.

cues.purpose: Two axes separate time latency from price slippage without conflating them.
cues.spoken_span: Slippage is price. Latency is time. Both can change an entry. Keeping the words separate helps us ask the right question about the test.

cues.purpose: Two axes separate time latency from price slippage without conflating them.
cues.spoken_span: A rule that needs the perfect entry has a timing weakness. This check makes that weakness visible. The weakness can be small in one trade and large across a population.

cues.purpose: A median-hour divider creates two session halves from the same trade stream.
cues.spoken_span: A split sample is a method that puts the same trades into separate groups before you measure them. The rule stays fixed; only the group used for the measurement changes.

cues.purpose: A median-hour divider creates two session halves from the same trade stream.
cues.spoken_span: The middle entry hour divides this intraday run into session half 1 and session half 2. That boundary gives both groups a declared place in the day.

cues.purpose: A median-hour divider creates two session halves from the same trade stream.
cues.spoken_span: A session half is one of those groups. It tells us whether the result leans on one part of the day. A strong combined result can hide a weak morning or afternoon group.

cues.purpose: A median-hour divider creates two session halves from the same trade stream.
cues.spoken_span: The rule keeps a candidate when profit factor clears 1.0 after the fill move and in both session halves. One candidate must clear the fill check plus both clock checks.

cues.purpose: Clock segments are shown as conditions that can carry or weaken a result.
cues.spoken_span: A regime is a stretch of market behavior. One rule can meet a different market in a different stretch. One stretch can trend, while another moves sideways or changes speed.

cues.purpose: Clock segments are shown as conditions that can carry or weaken a result.
cues.spoken_span: Price and volume can change across the trading day. Session splitting gives us a way to check that change. It asks whether the result travels with the clock instead of with the rule.

cues.purpose: Clock segments are shown as conditions that can carry or weaken a result.
